summary:
Lumen is a digital astronaut companion that supports the psychological wellbeing of astronauts during long-duration space missions. NASA’s Human Research Program has identified behavioural health, inadequate sleep and isolation as some of the greatest risks to health during spaceflight. During a multi-year mission to Mars, communication with Earth will be delayed by several minutes, meaning that astronauts will not be able to call their families or a doctor whenever they are struggling.

Each morning, astronauts complete a short check-in quiz about their sleep. During the day, they can read messages from family and friends, and send text and video messages. Each message will show the actual delay time as calculated by NASA JPL Horizons using the current distance between Earth and Mars. In the evening, a short gamified quiz on mood, energy, food, social contact and tasks helps them wind down and builds mood trends over time, so that a decline can be noticed early. Familiar backgrounds, local weather and news from home help Earth feel closer.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lumen follows the astronaut through a typical mission day:

  • 07:00, daily check-in: a short check-in on how the astronaut slept.
  • 07:02, message from home: a note from loved ones to keep morale up.
  • 12:30, send a message home: the astronaut types or records a short clip for loved ones on Earth. Each message shows its real travel delay, using NASA JPL Horizons data for the Earth–Mars distance and one-way light time.
  • 20:00, wind down: a short gamified quiz on mood, energy, food, social contact and tasks, with mood trends shown over time.

The app is personalised with backgrounds from the astronaut’s home country, plus local weather and news, so home feels closer.

Benefits

  • Gives astronauts a daily moment to pause and reflect on how they’re feeling.
  • Turns daily answers into trends, so a gradual decline in mood, sleep or energy shows up early, when it is easier to address.
  • Keeps astronauts connected to loved ones and life on Earth, countering isolation and confinement.
  • Makes communication delay visible, so both sides know when to expect a reply.

Intended impact
As missions get longer and travel farther from Earth, crews will rely more on themselves to manage their mental health. Lumen supports that self-awareness and keeps a sense of home within reach. The same approach could help people working in isolated places on Earth, such as Antarctic research stations or offshore crews.

NASA data and evidence

  • Dataset: NASA JPL Horizons System, for the Earth–Mars distance and one-way light time behind each message’s delay.
  • Evidence: each check-in topic maps to a named NASA spaceflight risk: mood (Risk of Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders), sleep and energy (Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules), meals (Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to Inadequate Food and Nutrition), and messages and news from home (Hazard: Isolation and Confinement).

Tools used

  • Figma for the app design and interactive prototype.
  • NASA JPL Horizons for Earth–Mars light-time data.
  • ChatGPT for image generation.
  • Google Slides for the presentation.
  • React (Vite) and TypeScript for the frontend web application.
  • Vercel for website deployment and hosting.

Creativity
Most astronaut health tools focus on physical health: vitals, the environment, exercise and diet. Lumen puts the mind first, addressing what exercise and diet can’t fix: missing home. Using real NASA orbital data to show the delay on each message turns the distance from Earth into something the astronaut can feel, and the gamified wind-down quiz makes reflecting on wellbeing a habit rather than a chore.

Factors we considered

  • Time: check-ins take minutes, so they fit around a busy mission schedule.
  • Honest reporting: the gamification rewards completing check-ins, not “good” answers, so astronauts have no reason to hide how they feel.
  • Distance from Earth: the app works around communication delays rather than assuming real-time contact.
  • Ease of use: short questions in plain language, no medical training needed.
  • Evidence: every tracked topic is grounded in NASA Human Research Program research.
